title: Validate a CAN Message's Rolling Counter and Checksum
statement:
A CAN bus can drop a frame, deliver a stale one twice, or corrupt a bit in
transit, and the bus itself will not tell you any of that happened. Safety-
relevant signals defend against it end-to-end: every frame carries a rolling
**alive counter** and a **checksum**, and the receiver's job is to notice
when either one is wrong and hold the last trusted value rather than act on
a frame it cannot vouch for.

This exercise uses a 4-bit counter (wrapping `0`-`15`) and a whole-frame XOR
checksum -- simplified from a real protocol, but the shape of the check is
the same one AUTOSAR's E2E profiles use.

## Your function

```
int can_e2e_check(const unsigned char *data, int length, int counter,
                  int received_checksum, int last_good_counter);
```

`last_good_counter` is the counter value from the last frame **this
function accepted** -- or `-1` if there has not been one yet. Return `1` to
accept the frame, `0` to reject it. To accept:

1. Recompute the checksum: start from `counter`, XOR in every byte of `data`
   in order, and compare the result to `received_checksum`. A mismatch is an
   automatic reject.
2. If `last_good_counter` is `-1`, this is the first frame ever seen and any
   counter value starts the sequence. Otherwise the counter must equal
   `(last_good_counter + 1) % 16` -- anything else means a frame was
   dropped, duplicated, or reordered.

The harness keeps `last_good_counter` for you between calls, and only
advances it when you return `1` -- your function itself holds no state.

## Watch out

- **The counter is part of the checksum.** Two frames with identical
  payload data but different counters must produce different checksums, so
  the check has to start from `counter`, not just XOR the payload bytes on
  their own -- an implementation that forgets the counter still catches
  payload corruption, but it stops catching a frame replayed with a stale
  counter and a payload that happens not to have changed.
- **A rejected frame must not move the baseline.** After a frame fails
  either check, the next incoming frame is still compared against the last
  *accepted* counter, not the bad one. One of the fixed tests sends a good
  frame, a corrupted one, and then a good frame that only makes sense
  counted from before the corrupted one arrived at all -- if your function
  is stateful on its own rather than trusting `last_good_counter`, or the
  harness's bookkeeping is misread, this is where it shows.
- The counter wraps: `15` is followed by `0`, not by a reject.

tests.name: a clean run of four frames
the counter rolls over from 15 to 0
a corrupted frame does not move the baseline
tests.description: Frame 3's checksum does not match at all and is rejected. Frame 4 carries counter 2, which is only valid counted from frame 2's counter of 1 -- proving frame 3 never became the new baseline.

tests.name: a valid checksum but a skipped counter
tests.description: The second frame's checksum is entirely correct for counter 3 -- it fails only because the sequence jumped from 1 to 3.

tests.name: the very first frame accepts any counter
tests.description: last_good_counter is -1 -- there is no prior frame to compare against yet.
